title: A community takes shape
text: Muhammad’s preaching in Mecca and the migration to Medina in 622 are central to the emergence of the Muslim community. By his death in 632, the movement had become a religious and political force in Arabia.

region: Arabia, the Levant, Iraq and Egypt
title: Expansion beyond Arabia
text: Under Abu Bakr and Umar, the caliphate consolidated power in Arabia and expanded into lands previously governed by the Byzantine and Sasanian empires. Territorial expansion and the gradual adoption of Islam are distinct historical processes.

title: Trade, pilgrimage, and learning
text: Trans-Saharan connections linked West African societies with North Africa. Mansa Musa’s pilgrimage through Cairo in 1324 and his patronage of scholarship illustrate the roles of rulers, travel, and learning in these networks.

title: A traveller encounters connected communities
text: Ibn Battuta’s Rihla describes a world linked by pilgrimage, legal learning, hospitality, and Muslim courts. His account is evidence of connections between communities, not a precise map of when entire populations converted.
source: UC Berkeley ORIAS — The Travels of Ibn Battuta

title: Institutions in the city
text: Sinan’s Selimiye complex at Edirne brings together worship, education, and commercial space. Such institutions show how Muslim religious and social life became embedded in urban settings.
source: UNESCO — Selimiye Mosque and its Social Complex

title: Two billion Muslims in the measured population
text: Pew Research Center estimates that the global Muslim population grew from 1.7 billion in 2010 to 2.0 billion in 2020. Its analysis attributes much of the growth to a younger population and higher fertility. These figures measure population change, not simply conversion.
source: Pew Research Center — Muslim population change

title: A living history, with dated evidence
text: The project’s research horizon reaches 2026. Historical accounts and demographic findings retain their own dates. The 2020 population estimate is not relabelled as a 2026 count, and projections are not presented as observed facts.
source: Pew Research Center — scope and dated findings
